title: Present perfect and past simple: finished and unfinished time
summary: Choose between the present perfect and past simple by checking whether the time period reaches the present or has finished. Practise yesterday, ago, this week, since, when-questions and past periods of residence or employment.
learningObjectives: Use the past simple with specific finished past times such as yesterday, last week and two years ago.
Use the present perfect to report experiences or events within an unfinished time period.
Use past-simple when-questions to ask about the time of a completed event.
Distinguish periods that continue to now from completed periods of work, residence and experience.

explanation.heading: Finished times take a past tense
explanation.body: Use past simple when a past event is tied to a time period that is finished. Expressions such as yesterday, last Tuesday, in 2018 and an hour ago refer to completed past times. Do not combine the present perfect with such a finished-time phrase in a standard sentence.
explanation.example: The supplier delivered the chairs last Thursday.

explanation.heading: Questions about when something happened
explanation.body: We normally use the past simple to ask when or at what time an event occurred. A present-perfect question can ask whether something has happened at all, but when did it happen? asks for a specific past-time detail.
explanation.example: “Have the guests arrived?” “Yes.” “When did they arrive?”

explanation.heading: Periods that include now
explanation.body: Use the present perfect to report what has happened within a period continuing until the moment of speaking, such as this week, today or this year. A period like this morning can be unfinished if it is still morning, but finished if it is now afternoon. The context determines the time boundary.
explanation.example: It is only eleven, and I have already answered twelve messages this morning.

explanation.heading: Contrasting ongoing and completed periods
explanation.body: Use the present perfect for situations that began earlier and still continue; use the past simple when the entire period is over. Since introduces a starting point continuing to now in the relevant present-perfect meaning; from 2012 to 2017 identifies a completed interval.
explanation.example: He has worked here since 2021, but he worked at a hotel from 2017 to 2020.

explanation.heading: Experience across a lifetime or a closed period
explanation.body: Have you ever…? and I have never… commonly refer to life experience up to now. Past simple can express what someone did or never did during a specific finished time, such as childhood. A completed holiday is described with a past tense; while the holiday is still in progress, present perfect is often suitable for an evaluation so far.
explanation.example: I have never travelled by ferry, but my brother travelled by ferry frequently when he was a student.

left.label: Unfinished period
left.example: We have held three meetings this week.
left.note: The present week is still in progress.

right.label: Finished period
right.example: We held three meetings last week.
right.note: Last week has ended, so past simple is appropriate.

left.label: Still true
left.example: Lena has lived in the same flat since 2020.
left.note: Her residence began in 2020 and continues now.

right.label: No longer true
right.example: Lena lived in another flat from 2016 to 2020.
right.note: The earlier period of residence is complete.

examples.sentence: Did you see the documentary on television yesterday?
examples.note: Yesterday is a finished past period, so ask with did.

examples.sentence: The repairs have taken longer than expected this week.
examples.note: The speaker is discussing a week that has not ended.

examples.sentence: When did the new café open?
examples.note: The question requests a specific past time.

examples.sentence: I have worked at this school since 2022.
examples.note: Present perfect indicates a period of employment continuing now.

examples.sentence: I never learnt to swim when I was a child.
examples.note: A finished period of life makes the past simple natural.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I have posted the letter yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: Yesterday is a finished time, so use past simple.

commonMistakes.incorrect: When have you joined the club?
commonMistakes.correct: When did you join the club?
commonMistakes.why: Ask about the date of a completed event with did.

commonMistakes.incorrect: She worked here since 2021 and she still works here.
commonMistakes.correct: She has worked here since 2021 and she still works here.
commonMistakes.why: A period that continues to the present calls for the present perfect.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We have lived in Spain from 2013 to 2016. We moved away after that.
commonMistakes.correct: We lived in Spain from 2013 to 2016. We moved away after that.
commonMistakes.why: The interval from 2013 to 2016 is completed, so use past simple.

studyTips: Draw a timeline: mark whether the named time period has ended before choosing the tense.
Practise pairs with changed time expressions: “today / yesterday”, “this year / last year”, “since 2021 / from 2017 to 2021”.
When you ask a question with when or what time, check that you are using did + base verb rather than have + participle.

exercises.prompt: It is still the middle of the week. For a progress report, choose the sentence that focuses on results so far.
choices: We have completed four lessons this week.
We completed four lessons last week.
We will complete four lessons next week.
exercises.feedback: Have completed this week focuses on progress during a time period that is still open.

exercises.prompt: The electrician ___ at eight o’clock yesterday morning.
exercises.feedback: At eight o’clock yesterday morning specifies a finished past time.

exercises.prompt: The concert finished at ten. Which question asks for the exact time it finished?
exercises.feedback: When did…finish? uses past simple to ask for a past time.

exercises.prompt: The exhibition is still running. It ___ more than five thousand visitors since it opened.
exercises.feedback: Has attracted describes a total measured over a period continuing until now.

exercises.prompt: We ___ (meet) the new director last Friday. Write the past-simple verb.
exercises.feedback: Last Friday is a finished past time, so use met.

exercises.prompt: I ___ (not / read) the latest message yet, and I still need to reply. Write the present-perfect negative verb phrase.
exercises.feedback: The message remains unread now, so use the present perfect negative.

exercises.prompt: The students ___ (not / attend) the workshop last summer. Write the past-simple negative verb phrase.
exercises.feedback: Last summer is over, so use did not + base verb.

exercises.prompt: Nora ___ (live) in Dublin from 2010 to 2016, but she lives elsewhere now. Write the past-simple verb.
exercises.feedback: From 2010 to 2016 is a completed period of residence.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I have met the course tutor three days ago.
acceptedAnswers: I met the course tutor three days ago.
exercises.feedback: Three days ago requires the past simple.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: When have you joined this organisation?
acceptedAnswers: When did you join this organisation?
exercises.feedback: When did you join? asks for the point in the past.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: She worked here since 2020 and she still works here.
acceptedAnswers: She has worked here since 2020 and she still works here.
She's worked here since 2020 and she still works here.
exercises.feedback: Since 2020 plus still shows the employment continues now.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I haven’t eaten breakfast yesterday.
acceptedAnswers: I did not eat breakfast yesterday.
exercises.feedback: Yesterday is a closed time period; use did not eat.

speakingExercises.prompt: State this completed event as one sentence: I / meet / Diana / on Monday. Use past simple and start “I”.
speakingExercises.feedback: Met is past simple because Monday identifies a finished occasion.

speakingExercises.prompt: It is still October. Say you have attended three seminars this month. Begin “I” and use present perfect.
acceptedAnswers: I have attended three seminars this month.
I've attended three seminars this month.
speakingExercises.feedback: This month is an unfinished time period; present perfect sums up progress so far.

speakingExercises.prompt: The museum did not open last week. Report this fact in one sentence beginning “The museum”.
acceptedAnswers: The museum did not open last week.
The museum didn't open last week.
speakingExercises.feedback: Did not open fits the finished period last week.

speakingExercises.prompt: You want the past date when an exhibition began. Ask one question beginning “When did” and ending “begin”.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use when did + base verb for a specific past-time question.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your uncle lived in Paris from 2015 to 2020 and has now moved away. Say one past-simple sentence beginning “My uncle” and ending “from 2015 to 2020”.
acceptedAnswers: My uncle lived in Paris from 2015 to 2020.
speakingExercises.feedback: The period from 2015 to 2020 is finished.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences using full forms. First: “I” + work here + since 2021, and I still work here. Second: before this job, “I” + work at a bakery. Start the second sentence with “Before that”.
acceptedAnswers: I have worked here since 2021. Before that, I worked at a bakery.
speakingExercises.feedback: Have worked is still true; worked describes a completed earlier job.

speakingExercises.prompt: It is eleven o’clock in the morning. You have finished two reports since breakfast. Say one sentence beginning “I” and ending “this morning”; use present perfect.
acceptedAnswers: I have finished two reports this morning.
I've finished two reports this morning.
speakingExercises.feedback: This morning has not ended, so present perfect is appropriate.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe your lifetime experience until now: I / never / visit / Canada. Start “I” and use present perfect.
speakingExercises.feedback: Have never visited refers to experience up to the present, not one finished period.

listeningExercises.audioText: It is only eleven in the morning, and I have already answered six enquiries today.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker mean about the six enquiries?
choices: They will answer all six tomorrow.
They answered them on a finished day last week.
They have answered them so far during the current day.
listeningExercises.feedback: Today still includes now, so have answered describes progress so far.

listeningExercises.audioText: We visited the aquarium on Tuesday and stayed there for two hours.
listeningExercises.prompt: When did the aquarium visit happen?
listeningExercises.feedback: Visited on Tuesday identifies a completed past event.

listeningExercises.audioText: I haven't had lunch today, and it is nearly one o'clock.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word negative verb phrase immediately after “I”, exactly as heard.
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker is still within today and has not yet eaten lunch.

listeningExercises.audioText: I worked in Madrid from 2014 to 2018. I now live and work in Valencia.
listeningExercises.prompt: What can we infer about the Madrid job?
choices: The speaker has held it since 2014 and still does.
The job ended before the move to Valencia.
The speaker will start it in 2018.
listeningExercises.feedback: From 2014 to 2018 is a completed past period.

listeningExercises.audioText: I have never swum in a lake, but I swam in the sea during my holiday last summer.
choices: The speaker swam in a lake last summer.
The speaker has never swum in the sea.
The speaker lacks lake experience but swam in the sea on a finished holiday.
listeningExercises.feedback: Have never refers to experience up to now; last summer identifies the past sea swim.

listeningExercises.audioText: We have not received any deliveries this week, but two boxes arrived last Friday.
listeningExercises.feedback: Arrived last Friday uses past simple for a closed time period.

listeningExercises.audioText: The concert ended at half past nine last night, and everyone left quietly.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single past-simple verb immediately after “The concert”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Ended is past simple because last night is over.

listeningExercises.audioText: We have studied together since September, and our course is still running.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word starting-point expression immediately after “together”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Since September indicates a period reaching the present.
